sec.title: Background
sec.p: The previous Italian national trial (AIEOP-AML-2002/01) on children with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) achieved a 3-year overall (OS) and event-free survival (EFS) of 72.3% and 59.1%, respectively. In this study (AIEOP-AML-2013), we evaluated if refined patient’s stratification in 3 groups and a second induction with randomization could improve outcomes.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In the new AIEOP-AML-2013, patients were stratified into 3 groups [standard-(SR), intermediate-(IR) and high-risk (HR)] mainly according to genetic criteria and centralized assessment of multiparametric flow-cytometry measurable residual disease (MFC-MRD). The 1st induction course was common for all patients [idarubicin-cytarabine-etoposide (ICE)]. IR and HR patients were then randomized to receive either a 2nd ICE or the fludarabine-cytarabine- liposomal-doxorubicin (FLA-My) scheme as second induction. IR patients with HLA-compatible sibling, and all HR patients were consolidated with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), while the remaining IR and SR patients were consolidated with chemotherapy only. Data cut-off was February 1, 2024.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: From June/2015 to June/2022, 371 patients were enrolled in the trial. Twenty-six children (7%) experienced primary induction failure, while only 3 patients died during the 2 induction courses. The cumulative incidence of 3-year non-relapse mortality in continuous complete remission was 6.8%. The proportion of patients allocated to the SR, IR, and HR groups were 19.5%, 22%, and 58.5%, respectively. Three-year cumulative incidence of relapse was 18.9%. The 3-year probabilities of OS and EFS were 83.9% and 68.5%, respectively, both values being significantly better (p = 0.001) than those of the AIEOP-AML-2002/01 study. The 3-year OS of SR, IR, and HR patients were 97.0%, 84.2%, and 79.4%, respectively, (p = 0.01). The probability of EFS did not differ in IR and HR randomized to receive either a 2nd ICE or the FLA-My scheme course. Levels of MRD after the 1st and 2nd induction course strongly influenced the EFS probability.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: A significant improvement in the outcomes of children with de novo AML was obtained with refined risk-stratification and risk-adapted therapy. FLA-My did not offer any advantage over repeating a 2nd ICE as 2nd induction course.

sec.title: Trial registration
sec.p: This study was registered in the European Clinical Trials Database (EudraCT 2014-000652-28).

sec.p: The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s13045-026-01798-3.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Outcomes of children newly diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) treated with first-line protocols have improved over the last decades, with a probability of 3 to 5-year overall survival (OS) and event-free survival (EFS) ranging from 65% to 75%, and from 45% to 57%, respectively [1–5]. This achievement was mainly based on a more precise biological characterization of the diseases resulting in fine-tuned risk stratification, use of allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) in first complete remission (CR1) for high-risk patients, and an improvement of the supportive care therapies [6, 7]. Over the last two decades, large-scale sequencing efforts have resulted in significant achievements in identifying several recurrent genetic lesions with prognostic impact, which also translates into potential therapeutic targets [8–10]. Moreover, multiparametric flow-cytometry (MFC) minimal/measurable residual disease (MRD) monitoring has emerged as a useful tool to stratify patients’ risk [11–13] and for specific subgroups, such as core-binding factor AML, quantitative genetic MRD screening enhances the stratification potential [14]. Nonetheless, disease relapse remains the major cause of treatment failure, with the cumulative incidence of disease recurrence ranging between 21% and 47% [1–5].

The Associazione Italiana di Ematologia ed Oncologia Pediatrica (AIEOP) conducted the first risk-based protocol in 2002, involving treatment intensification for high-risk patients [1] This resulted in a 8-yr EFS of 55% for the entire cohort, with disease-free survival (DFS) of 73% and 63% for patients receiving allogeneic or autologous HSCT, respectively [1, 15]. These results were comparable to those reported by other international collaborations, but with a longer follow-up and also a noteworthy rescue rate of the relapsed patients of 71% was reported [1, 6]. Building on that experience, non-Down pediatric patients with AML other than acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) have been enrolled in the AIEOP-AML-2013 protocol. The main aim of the study was to determine in a randomized fashion the most appropriate induction therapy using the liposomal formulation of doxorubicin, assess the role of MFC-MRD in disease stratification, and evaluate the benefit deriving from allo-HSCT in CR1 for patients with high (HR) and intermediate risk (IR). We here report the outcomes of children enrolled in this randomized trial.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: AIEOP-AML-2013/01 was an academic, multicenter protocol study conducted in 33 AIEOP sites in Italy (full list is reported in supplementary material) on risk-adapted chemotherapy treatment for pediatric patients (aged 0–18 years) with de-novo AML other than APL, including an open-label, randomized part for IR and HR patients. All pediatric patients diagnosed with AML in an AIEOP center were considered eligible; exclusion criteria were: (1) constitutional trisomy 21; (2) AML evolving from myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) or therapy-related AML; (3) having received any chemotherapy regimen or systemic steroids for more than 7 days; (4) any organ function impairment > grade 4 of the WHO scale, causing impossibility to adhere to the treatment schedule. Participants were stratified into 3 risk groups, namely standard risk (SR), IR, and HR, based on the molecular/cytogenetic characterization and values of MFC-MRD at the end of induction therapy (EOI). In particular, SR patients were defined by a core binding factor (CBF) or nucleophosmin 1 (NPM1) mutation and MRD < 0.1% at EOI1; HR were those with one or more of the following characteristics: (i) cytogenetic abnormalities known to be associated with dismal prognosis (including complex or monosomal karyotype, most of KMT2A-rearrangments, rare abnormalities like t(5;11) NUP98::NSD1) (full list and more details on risk stratification are reported in supplementary Table 1); (ii) FLT3 internal tandem duplication (ITD); (iii) cryptic inversion of chromosome 16 leading to CBFA2T3::GLIS2 fusion gene; (iv) French–American–British (FAB) classification M0, M6, and M7 [with the exclusion of cases with t(1;22) RBM15::MKL1]; (v) patients below 1 year of age at diagnosis [infants, with the exclusion of cases with M7 and t(1;22)]; (vi) patients not in CR at the EOI (definition of response is reported in the supplementary material); (vii) patients with MRD ≥ 1% at EOI1 or ≥ 0.1% at EOI2; (viii) patients with hyperleukocytosis (i.e., > 100,000 WBC/mcl) at diagnosis and not classified as SR. IR patients were those not matching SR or HR definition.

The study was approved by the Ethical Committees of each participating center. Written informed consent was obtained by both parents or legal representatives before enrolment in accordance with regulatory guidelines; minors above the age of 12 were required to provide written assent. The study protocol is available online (supplementary material). The study was registered in EudraCT database as 2014-000652-28.

sec.title: Randomization and masking
sec.p: Following assessment of response to the first cycle of induction chemotherapy (idarubicin, cytarabine, and etoposide, ICE), all patients not stratified into the SR group were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive a second induction course with either a second ICE or the combination of fludarabine, cytarabine and liposomal doxorubicin (FLA-My).

Randomization was performed by the local investigator at each clinical site using an AIEOP, protocol-specific, electronic remote data entry system located at CINECA (Consorzio Interuniversitario Nazionale per il Calcolo Automatico, Casalecchio di Reno, BO, Italy). The clinical trial unit staff and the investigators and treating physicians in each clinical unit did not have access to the randomization list. The randomization code was generated by nQuery Advisor using a block randomization scheme and a block size of four. Randomization was open-label; all investigators were aware of the treatment allocation.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: Diagnosis of AML was performed/confirmed centrally at the Pediatric Onco-Hematology Laboratory at the University of Padua according to the French-American-British (FAB) and WHO classification criteria. Samples were processed and analyzed according to standardized operating procedures (SOP) previously described [16]. The whole immunophenotypic characterization was performed at diagnosis according to WHO criteria, using a direct immunofluorescence technique with 8–12 color combinations of monoclonal antibodies. Regarding the genetic characterization, for all AML samples at diagnosis RNA was extracted from mononuclear cells isolated by density gradient using Lymphoprep™ (Stemcell Technologies, Vancouver, BC, Canada). Total RNA extraction and reverse transcription was performed by using one microgram RNA reverse-transcribed into cDNA using SuperScript II (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). All patients were screened for 41 different molecular markers by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) with specific primers previously validated to detect the molecular lesions [7, 9, 10, 17, 18]. Shifted primers were used to confirm the positivity of the rearrangement/mutation and to define the breakpoint for each case. Moreover, for all cases, karyotyping or FISH were performed.

Once the diagnosis was confirmed, all patients received the ICE course through a central venous line; details on treatment course and schemes are reported in Fig. 1A and supplementary Tables 2 and 3 (including a comparison with the previous protocol, AIEOP-AML-2002).

caption.p: Protocol outline. APL, acute promyelocytic leukemia; DS, Down syndrome; EOI, end of induction timepoint.

sec.p: Hematological response was performed locally at hematological recovery, while monitoring of MFC-MRD on bone marrow (BM) aspirate at EOI1 and EOI2 was centrally performed, according to the European Leukemia Network guidelines [19] with adaptations for pediatric AML [20]. The samples were stained using a dual tube approach with customized dried format antibody cocktail tubes (DuraCloneTM, Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA) [21]. The approach allows for MRD detection in AML by leukemia-associated immunophenotype (LAIP), as well as by different-from-normal assessment, since LAIPs are not always reliable and sensitive for MRD monitoring due to several reasons (e.g., expressed only by a subpopulations of blast cells, not stable during follow-up, etc.). Both tubes were run at diagnosis, and during follow-up. Data files were analyzed independently by at least two reviewers. Positive MRD was accepted in the case of a minimum of 50 clustered cellular events resembling the LAIP determined at diagnosis, and/or unambiguously different from normal.

After the first induction, SR patients were treated with 3 additional chemotherapy courses, all including high-dose cytarabine (HD-Ara-C) (Mitoxantrone, Cytarabine, and Etoposide, short MEC; Cytarabine and Etoposide, AVE; Cytarabine and Mitoxantrone, HAM). After a planned interim analysis showing a higher-than-expected incidence of relapse, the protocol was amended to add a 5th cycle of HD-Ara-C for SR patients. After 1st induction, IR and HR patients were randomized to receive either a 2nd ICE or the FLA-My scheme as 2nd induction course. IR pts were then given 3 additional consolidation courses (AVE, HAM, and fludarabine, cytarabine, and amsacrine, FLAMSA) or, in the presence of an HLA-compatible sibling, 1 consolidation course (AVE) followed by allo-HSCT. Finally, patients of the HR group were consolidated with 2 additional chemotherapy courses (AVE and HAM) and, then, had an indication to receive allo-HSCT from either a donor compatible for ≥ 9/10 HLA loci or from an HLA-partially matched family donor (PMFD). Primary induction failure (PIF) was defined as > 25% blasts at EOI1 or > 5% blasts at EOI2. At every cycle of chemotherapy, irrespectively of central nervous system (CNS) status, patients received intrathecal (IT) therapy with age-adjusted cytarabine, methotrexate and steroids; patients with CNS disease involvement at diagnosis received, during the 1st induction additional IT treatments (every 3 days) until disease clearance. Salvage treatment (after PIF or 1st relapse) was not specified by protocol and was left to treating physician decision. In general, fludarabine + cytarabine, with or without idarubicin or gemtuzumab ozogamicin (if blasts were CD33+), were widely used; this kind of treatment remained broadly adopted during the years, since no new treatment for AML became available in the study period. All patients in CR2 or after PIF had an indication to allogeneic HSCT. Regarding the conditioning regimen for allo-HSCT, the recommended one was busulfan + cyclophosphamide + melphalan in case of transplant from an HLA-matched donor, while, in case of PMFD, the choice was left to the treating physician. The recommended conditioning regimen did not differ for patients with extramedullary disease.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary endpoint was an improvement of 5% of 3-year EFS as compared to the previous national protocol for AML (AIEOP-AML-2002/01).1 Secondary endpoints were: (i) to evaluate the applicability of MFC-MRD monitoring after the 1st and 2nd induction (percentage of patients successfully monitored) and its prognostic role (difference in OS and EFS between patients with high or low MFC-MRD after the 2 induction cycles); (ii) to reduce the number of early deaths (ED) and deaths in continuous complete remission (CCR) as compared to AIEOP-AML-2002/01; (iii) to evaluate the prognostic value of the new risk stratification algorithm (difference in OS and EFS of the 3 risk groups); (iv) to evaluate if a reduction of about 20% of the cumulative chemotherapy doses in the SR group was associated with a superimposable outcome as compared to previous protocol and the other risk groups of the current protocol (comparison of OS and EFS of SR patients with those of SR patients treated in AIEOP-AML-2002/01 and those of IR and HR of the current protocol); (v) to evaluate the therapeutic role of the FLAMSA cycle in IR patients who lacked a matched family donor (MFD) (difference in OS and EFS of IR patients treated with FLAMSA or transplanted from a MFD donor); (vi) to evaluate the efficacy of transplantation from a matched unrelated donor (MUD) or an haploidentical donor (PMFD) in CR1 HR patients in case of lacking of a MFD (comparison of OS and EFS of patients transplanted from MFD, MUD or PFMD); (vii) to describe the infectious complications of patients enrolled in the trial.

Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 4.0 was used to grade all adverse events (AE). Both AEs and serious AEs (SAE) were assessed and judged by the investigators to be related or not to the study drugs. A data safety monitoring board reviewed and analyzed on an annual basis safety data; in case of unexpected or unacceptable toxicities the members had the authority to recommend the discontinuation of the study. Additionally, a data monitoring committee composed by the protocol PI and 2 site PI monitored the conduction of the study.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: We hypothesized that the new risk stratification system, coupled with risk-adjusted intensification of consolidation treatment could result into an improvement of 5% of 3-year EFS compared with the previous national protocol. We estimated a sample size of 360 patients considering a power of 0.80 and α equal to 0.05 to reject the null hypothesis in a log-rank test model. Moreover, for the randomized question, we hypothesized an increase of the percentage of patients with MFC-MRD < 0.1% at the end of the second induction from 65% after 2 ICE schemes (as in the previous protocol) to 85% after ICE and FLA-My (experimental arm). With a α of 0.05 and a power of 0.80 we calculated a sample size of 83 patients per arm.

OS was calculated from date of diagnosis to time of death due to any cause or time of last follow-up. EFS was calculated from date of diagnosis to first event (failure to achieve CR, relapse, second malignancy, or death due to any cause, whichever occurred first) or last follow-up. DFS was calculated from the date of remission to last follow-up or first event (relapse, second malignancy, or death due to any cause, whichever occurred first). Probabilities of OS, EFS, and DFS were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Cumulative incidence (CI) of relapse and death in continuous complete remission (CCR) were estimated taking into consideration for the respective competing risks. Death in CCR was treated as a competing event to calculate CI of relapse, while relapse was considered the competing event for death in CCR. The significance of differences among the OS, EFS, and DFS curves was estimated by the log-rank test (Mantel-Cox). In order to try to dissect the role of allogeneic HSCT on outcomes data, sensitivity analyses with censoring at transplantation were performed. For the multivariable analysis on EFS the Cox proportional regression model was used. Analyses were performed using EZR version 1.32 (Saitama Medical Centre, Jichi Medical University), which is a graphical user interface for R (The R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). All analyses were performed as intention-to-treat. Data cut-off for this analysis was February 1, 2024. This study was registered in the European Clinical Trials Database (EudraCT 2014-000652-28; https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/trial/2014-000652-28/IT).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Between May/2015 and June/2022, 371 patients were enrolled in the trial. Figure 1 reports trial consort diagram and Fig. 2 patients’ disposition, while Tables 1 and 2 show patients characteristics of the whole study population (Table 1) and of patients who underwent randomization (Table 2).

sec.p: Age distribution and disease characteristics were in line with those reported in other studies, in particular with patients enrolled in the AIEOP-AML-2002/01 protocol (Table 3) [1, 6].

caption.p: Comparison of patients’ characteristics enrolled in the current (AIEOP-AML-2013) and previous (AIEOP-AML-2002) study

sec.p: At time of diagnosis, we identified a molecular lesion in 248 cases (67% of the 371) (Supplementary material and Supplementary Fig. 1). According to disease characteristics and response to induction therapy, 72 patients (19.5%) were allocated to SR group, while 81 (22%) and 218 (58.5%) to the IR and HR groups, respectively. Overall, 92% (342 out of 371) of patients obtained morphological CR at the end of the 2 induction courses, as compared to 87% (421/482) of the previous AIEOP –AML-2002/01 study (p = 0.02) [1]. In details, all SR and IR patients reached CR, while 189/218 (86.7%) HR patients did so. Three patients (1%), all belonging to the HR group, died in induction, as compared to 13 (3%) of the previous AIEOP-AML-2002/01 study protocol (p = 0.03).

With a median follow-up of 64 months for surviving patients (range 18–104), the 3-year OS, EFS and DFS of the whole cohort were 83.9% (95% CI 79.5–87.4), 68.5% (95% CI 63.4–73.1), and 74.3% (95% CI 69.1–78.7), respectively (Fig. 3A and supplementary Fig. 2 A, 2B). The primary endpoint was met; indeed, the 3-year EFS of the current protocol was higher than that of the previous protocol (AIEOP-AML-2002/01), the difference being 9.4% (95% CI 0.3–18.5; p = 0.002) (Fig. 3B).

caption.p: (A) Overall survival (OS) of the whole cohort. (B) Event-free survival (EFS) of the current (AIEOP-AML-2013, grey line) and the previous (AIEOP-AML-2002/01, red line) protocol. (C) OS by risk group. (D) EFS of IR/HR patients by random

sec.p: The risk stratification system was accurate in predicting outcome, since the 3-year OS of SR, IR, and HR patients were 97.0%, 84.2%, and 79.4%, respectively (Fig. 3C, p = 0.01). Notably, DFS did not differ between the 3 risk groups (supplementary Fig. 3 A).

Two hundred and fifty-eight IR and HR patients were randomized to receive either a 2nd ICE or the FLA-My scheme (Table 2). Patients receiving ICE or FLA-My had a similar 3-year EFS of 70.3% and 74.6% respectively (p = 0.43; Fig. 3D). Further post-hoc subgroup analyses of specific cohorts, including infants, patients with a KMT2A-rearrangement, FLT3-ITD, CBFA2T3::GLIS2 mutation, IR only or HR only and M6/M7 failed to identify superior outcomes for either therapies (supplementary Table 4). Additionally, there was no difference in terms of MRD response (MFC-MRD < 0.1%) at EOI2 between the control arm (101/129, 78% of patients) and the experimental arm (106/129, 82% of patients) (p = n.s.). Also after sensitivity analysis (with censoring at transplantation), there was no difference in terms of OS and EFS, between the 2 arms of the randomized question (data not shown). Although the reduction of dose intensity in SR patients as compared to the previous protocol (see also supplementary Table 3) was not associated with a reduction in OS or EFS (3-year OS 97.0% vs. 87.5%, p = 0.1, and 70.6% vs. 66.3%. p = 0.3, respectively), EFS of this risk group was lower than that of IR patients in the current protocol (3-year EFS of SR, IR, and HR patients 70.6%, 75.6%, and 65.0%, respectively; p = 0.02, supplementary Fig. 3B). Sensitivity analyses on OS and EFS with censoring at transplant are reported in the supplementary material (supplementary Fig. 3 C and 3D). Despite the addition of a 5th cycle (HD-ARAc) after an amendment of the protocol, the EFS of SR patients did not improve (supplementary Fig. 4). We also performed a post-hoc analysis to test the hypothesis whether the higher the number of criteria for HR, the worst the prognosis was; notably, 3-year EFS of patients with either 1 or 2 or ≥ 3 risk factors was remarkably different [80.2% (95% CI 71.2–86.7), 58.3% (45.3–69.2), and 35.7% (95% CI 21.7–49.9), respectively, p < 0.0001, supplementary Fig. 5).

Eighty-one IR patients were in CR after the 2nd induction and received consolidation therapy (i.e., AVE, HAM, and FLAMSA or AVE and HSCT in case of availability of a MFD). All IR patients who received a HSCT in first CR are alive and disease-free. In contrast, the IR patients consolidated with chemotherapy had a 3-year OS and EFS of 85.0% (95% CI, 73.1–91.9) and 75.9% (95% CI, 63.2–84.7), respectively; this difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.18 and p = 0.08, respectively, supplementary Fig. 6 A and 6B).

Three hundred and fifty-eight patients (97.2% of evaluable patients) and 331 (94.8% of evaluable patients) were monitored for MFC-MRD at EOI1 and EOI2, respectively. At both time-points, MFC-MRD was significantly associated with outcomes; indeed, as shown in Fig. 4A and B, the 3-year EFS difference between patients with MFC-MRD above and below 0.1% was 28.4% (95% CI 12.1–44.7, p < 0.0001) at EOI1 and 27.2% (95% CI 0–56.4.4, p < 0.0001) at EOI2. Notably, when measurement at EOI1 and EOI2 were combined, there was a significant difference between the 3 groups (i.e., patients with MFC-MRD below 0.1% at both EOI1 and EOI2, patients with MFC-MRD above 0.1% at EOI1 but below 0.1% at EOI2 and patients with MFC-MRD above 0.1% at both EOI1 and EOI2) (p < 0.0001, Fig. 4 C).

caption.p: A. EFS by MFC-MRD at end of induction 1 (EOI1). B. EFS by MFC-MRD at end of induction 2 (EOI2). C. EFS by MFC-MRD at EOI1&EOI2. D. cumulative incidence of relapse and death in continuous complete remission (CCR)

sec.p: Exploratory analysis on the role of quantitative PCR (qPCR)-MRD for NPM1 and CBF-mutated SR patients were performed: while there was no prognostic value for NPM1-mutated patients and those with inv(16) at both EOI1 and EOI2 using different thresholds, patients with t(8;21) reducing qPCR-MRD more than 3 Log at EOI2 had an improved EFS (81.5% vs. 26.7%, p = 0.07; supplementary Fig. 7).

Of the 342 patients who achieved CR after the 2 induction courses, 65 relapsed at a median time of 390 days from diagnosis (IQR 255–546) and 221 days from the end of treatment (IQR 228–546), the 3-year cumulative incidence of relapse being 18.9% (95% CI 14.8–23.4) (Fig. 4D). Of these 65 patients, 57 (88%) had an isolated BM relapse, while 4 (6%) had an isolated extramedullary relapse and 4 (6%) a combined relapse. Of these patients, 38 (58.4%) are alive at last follow-up. CNS status at diagnosis did not significantly impact on outcome (data not shown). Twenty-three patients (1 allocated to SR, 7 to IR, and 15 to HR group) died in CCR (8 after HSCT), mainly due to infectious complications (supplementary Table 5), the 3-year cumulative incidence of treatment-related mortality being 6.8% (95% CI 4.5–9.9) (Fig. 4D). Table 4 reports details on toxicities according to treatment arm allocation (including 3rd and 4th cycles).

caption.p: Toxicities, according to CTCAE version 4.0, of the 2 treatment arm

fn.p: For grade 1–2, only events with a frequency > 10% are reported. All grade 3, 4 and 5 events are reported. Absolute numbers (and percentages) are reported

sec.p: Regarding other safety/toxicity data, given the type of the chemotherapy courses, no patients required dose reductions nor treatment discontinuation because of toxicity. However, because of severe infections during the treatment course (e.g., sepsis by multi-drug resistant bacteria), not all patients received the planned chemotherapy cycles; in details (see also Fig. 1B): (i) 2 non-SR patients were not randomized and were thus treated with a conventional second ICE; (ii) 3 patients in the HR group did not receive HSCT as consolidation. Serious adverse events were common in both randomization arms, sepsis/febrile neutropenia causing prolonged hospitalization being the most common event [78 (60.4%) in ICE arm vs. 70 (54.2%) in FLA-My arm, p = n.s.].

One hundred and seventy patients (158 HR, 12 IR) underwent allo-HSCT in CR1. The donor was a MFD for 45 patients (26.5%), a UD for 67 (39.5%), and a PMFD for 58 (34%). The recommended conditioning regimen was busulfan + cyclophosphamide + melphalan in case of transplant from an HLA-matched donor (87.4% of patients received the recommended conditioning), while, in case of PMFD, the choice was left to the treating physician (in 36% of cases busulfan + cyclophosphamide + melphalan was used, while regarding the other patients, 15.5% received busulfan + thiotepa + fludarabine, 17.2% a TBI-based approach, 17.2% a treosulfan-based regimen and the remaining 14.1% other combinations). Three-year OS and EFS after HSCT were 90.4% (95% CI 84.5–94.1, supplementary Fig. 8 A) and 84.6% (95% CI 78.0–89.4.0.4, supplementary Fig. 8B). Although there was no difference in OS after HSCT based on donor type (supplementary Fig. 8 C), EFS differed, with HSCT from MFD showing the best outcome (supplementary Fig. 8D); however, after removing IR patients transplanted from MFD, this difference became no longer significant (p = 0.07).

Subgroup analysis showed encouraging outcomes for specific difficult-to-treat patients. In details, 28 infants (i.e. < 1 year of age) were treated within the protocol; 10 (37.5%) were KMT2A-rearranged, 2 had a t(1;22) RBM15::MKL1, while 1 each had a t(16;16) CBFA2T3::GLIS2, a t(2;11) NUP98::HOXD13, and a t(7;12) MNX1::ETV6. The 3-year OS and EFS of infant patients were 89.1% (95% CI 70.0–96.4.0.4) and 78.3% (95% CI 57.8–89.6), respectively. The 3-year OS of patients with FLT3-ITD (N = 22 without other mutations) and KMT2A-rearranged leukemia (N = 67) were 90.9% (95% CI 68.3–97.6) and 79.8% (95% CI 67.0–88.1.0.1), while the 3-year EFS of the same subgroups were 63.6% (95% CI 40.3–79.9) and 69.4% (95% CI 56.6–79.1), respectively. Notably, the 3-year EFS of the 32 patients with either t(6;11) KMT2A::AFDN or t(10:11) KMT2A::MLLT10 was 68.3% (95% CI 49.0–81.5.0.5). The 3-year outcomes of other high-risk subgroups of interest (namely 15 NUP98-rearranged, 9 CBFA2T3::GLIS2 patients and 35 with M6/M7 AML) were as follows: for NUP98-rearranged, OS 92.3% (95% CI 56.6–98.9) and EFS 53.3% (95% CI 26.3–74.4); for CBFA2T3::GLIS2, both OS and EFS were equal at 3 years (44.4%; 95% CI 13.6–71.9); for M6/M7, OS 82.4% (95% CI 64.9–91.7) and EFS 71.1% (95% CI 52.9–83.3). Finally, the 3-yr OS of patients experiencing PIF was 70.6% (95% CI 47.4–85.0).

In a multivariable model for OS and EFS (Table 5) including cytogenetics, MFC-MRD, age < 1 year at diagnosis and hyperleukocytosis at onset, only MFC-MRD remained statistically significant (HR 1.52 and 1.71 for OS and EFS, respectively; p < 0.0001).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This AIEOP-AML-2013 academic, multicenter risk-adapted protocol achieved a 3-year OS and EFS of 83.9% and 68.5%, respectively, both being significantly improved as compared to the previous AIEOP-AML-2002/01 protocol, in which the 3-year OS and EFS was 72.3% and 59.1%, respectively [1]. This improvement can be attributed to better patient allocation into risk groups, achieved through refined genetic characterization and MFC-MRD, as well as to advancements in supportive care (e.g., infection control; indeed, the 2 trials were run in 2 different decades, new antimicrobials becoming available in the more recent period). This hypothesis is supported by a low 3-year cumulative incidence of death in CCR (6.8%), suggesting that the therapeutic burden was appropriate without excessive toxicities. Notably, compared to the previous AIEOP study (i.e. AIEOP-AML-2002/01), the higher rate of morphological CR at the end of the induction and the extremely low percentage of patients experiencing death in induction support the interpretation that induction therapy was more effective and not associated with increased toxicity. In addition, patients treated in the current protocol had a lower 3-year cumulative incidence of relapse, (18.9 vs. 25.6%, p = 0.01) indicating that the anti-leukemia activity was greater as compared to the previous AIEOP-AML-2002/01 study.

In the recent literature, some collaborative trials for the treatment of pediatric AML have been published, namely, AML-BFM 2012 study, the Children’s Oncology Group (COG) Trial AAML0531, the MyeChild 01, the Nordic Society for Pediatric Hematology and Oncology (NOPHO AML2012), and the Japanese Children’s Cancer Group JPLSG-AML-12 [22–26]. OS and EFS in our study were comparable to those reported by the other international protocols in the same study period such the AML-BFM 2012 Study (3-years OS and EFS of 82% and 69%) [22], the MyeChild 01 (2-years OS and EFS of 71% and 62%, respectively) [24], and the NOPHO AML2012 (OS and EFS of 79.6% and 66.7%, respectively) [25]. Rate of CR after induction was comparable to NOPHO study [25] but superior to the one reported in the MyeChild 01 study [24], with the rate of death in induction being lower to the one reported in the AML-BFM 2012 study [22].

Similar to other protocols, disease recurrence or primary resistance were the main causes of treatment failure. However, in our study, the probability of DFS did not differ among the three different risk groups. This suggests that tailoring consolidation therapy according to the risk profile was successful in improving the outcomes of patients with poorer prognostic characteristics. Specific consideration deserves the SR group in which we observed a higher relapse rate compared to the IR and HR (25% vs. 15% vs. 15%). However, while SR exhibited a higher relapse rate and a similar DFS compared to IR patients (70.6% vs. 75.6%), the 6-year OS was higher (91.6% vs. 84.2%), indicating that a higher proportion of SR patients can be salvaged by second-line treatment, including allogeneic HSCT. In light of the higher-than-expected number of relapse of the SR group in the ad interim analysis, we amended the protocol to add a 5th cycle of HD-Ara-C. However, the EFS survival did not improve after the amendment. Possible explanations for this finding are that SR patients experiencing relapse may have presented with a biologically different disease that was not controlled with an intensification of the consolidation treatment or that a more intense induction is needed also in SR patients.

HR patients, the most represented subset in our cohort, could be further stratified based on the number of HR features, as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 5. This suggests that disease classification could be further improved in identifying patients at very-high risk of worse outcome, particularly those with three or more features, who exhibit an OS lower than 40%. These patients should certainly deserve special consideration and novel treatment options for the disease control in the next protocols.

The AIEOP-AML-2013 randomized in a 1:1 ratio IR and HR patients to receive as 2nd induction the FLA-My scheme compared to the standard ICE. EFS in the two group was similar, indicating that FLA-My did not offer any advantage over repeating a 2nd ICE. This result corroborates the ones reported for the St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital AML08 trial in which the introduction of clofarabine to reduce daunorubicin exposure did not result in a different outcome in terms of CR rate, EFS and OS [27]. It is challenging to further improve such a high rate of morphological CR after induction therapy only with modifications of the standard chemotherapy schedule and the low number of patients experiencing a PIF may probably benefit from novel therapies to reach a CR, hopefully including in the future CAR T cells [28].

According to the protocol treatment schedule, patients in the IR group after the first cycle of consolidation received HSCT only from a MFD. It is noteworthy that patients receiving chemotherapy alone, due to the lack of a MFD experience, had a worse EFS (75.9% vs. 100.0%), although this difference did not reach statistical significance, likely due to the small number of patients.

This was the first Italian protocol integrating MFC-MRD in the risk stratification after the first and second induction course. The prognostic value of MFC-MRD on disease outcome has been previously demonstrated [12]. In our study, a centralized MFC-MRD evaluation was available for most of patients included in the protocol (97.2% at EOI1 and 94.8% at EOI2), confirming the broad applicability of this approach for monitoring treatment response in large protocols and similar to what was reported by other groups [12]. MFC-MRD values both at EOI1 and EOI2 with a 0.1% threshold significantly stratified patients in better and worse outcome as previously reported [12]. Interestingly, in our cohort the best prediction of the outcome using MFC-MRD was obtained by the combination of values at EOI1 and EOI2, supporting the idea of a dynamic evolution of the disease risk. The prominent role of MFC-MRD in predicting outcomes of pediatric de novo AML was further confirmed by the multivariable analysis. We also performed preliminary analyses on the role of qPCR-MRD in SR patients; in children with t(8;21), an at least 3-Log reduction of MRD EOI2 was associated with improved EFS (as also previously reported in a post-hoc analysis of AML 2002 protocol). For this reason, in the current AIEOP-BFM 2020 protocol (EurdaCT: 2022–500783-35-00), a specific criterion for SR classification has been implemented. We did not see an effect for inv(16) and NPM1 patients; for this latest group, however, it is now known that the type of mutation is associated with the outcome (type D mutations of NPM1 being significantly associated with inferior outcomes) [29].

In our study protocol, there was a wide use of allo-HSCT, since both all HR patients and IR patients with an available MFD had an upfront indication to the procedure, while, differently from the previous study, autologous HSCT was not used anymore. Although a similar proportion of patients in the 2 protocols received HSCT (46.8% in AML 2013 versus 50.4% in AML 2002, p = n.s.), more patients in the AML 2013 received an allograft (46.8% in AML 2013 versus 29.2% in AML 2002, p < 0.001) and this may have contributed to the improved survival recorded in AIEOP AML 2013. Both OS and EFS were remarkably high after HSCT, demonstrating the safety and the efficacy of transplantation also after an intense treatment course. Additionally, patients transplanted from a matched donor were largely treated with the same conditioning regimen (with more than 85% of patients receiving the recommended preparative course), this making the cohort a useful benchmark for future studies on HSCT in pediatric AML. In order to dissect the effect of HSCT on protocol outcomes, we run sensitivity analyses with censoring at transplant, confirming the value of our risk stratification system, as well as the role of HSCT in improving both EFS and OS of high-risk patients and in rescuing relapsed SR patients.

The outcome of specific subgroups, such as patient with FLT3-ITD and KMT2A-rearranged leukemia, was encouraging; worth to be noted that this was obtained without the use of approved or experimental specific inhibitors [30], which, in the future, may further improve survival of these patients.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In summary, our results demonstrate a significant improvement in the outcomes of children with de novo AML, as compared to the previous study to be mainly attributed to enhanced risk stratification and consequent tailored therapy. Indeed, FLA-My did not offer any advantage over repeating a 2nd ICE as 2nd induction course.

Patients with SR disease achieved an OS probability exceeding 90%, a result that rivals current outcomes for pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Future protocols should integrate novel therapies, such as demethylating agents [31], BCL2 inhibitors [32], menin-inhibitors [30] and cellular therapies [28], to further enhance these favorable results.
